content:
Seated exercise is one of the safest ways to keep moving with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) when standing is hard, and it helps on both bad and better days, as long as you change what you do to match how your joints are. During a flare, when joints are hot, swollen and tender, keep it gentle: slow range-of-movement exercises, little and often, letting the inflamed joints settle rather than pushing strength work. Between flares, build up gradually with seated strengthening and a little seated aerobic activity such as marching on the spot. Ask your rheumatology team for specialist physiotherapy, and for a hand exercise programme if your hands or wrists are a problem. Get help the same day if one joint becomes suddenly hot, swollen and very painful and you feel feverish or unwell, and never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is about adjusting seated exercise to rheumatoid arthritis, especially flare days. For a ready-made gentle routine, see chair yoga for stiff joints. For how hard strength work should feel and how to progress it, see seated strength exercises. To practise getting up from a chair, see sit-to-stand practice.

Why RA needs its own exercise plan

Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory condition. Your joints can be fine one week and hot, swollen and stiff the next. In osteoarthritis, steady exercise most days is usually the plan. With RA, the right amount changes with your disease activity, so one fixed routine rarely fits every week.

Exercise still matters. The National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society (NRAS) says physical activity helps people with all forms of arthritis. NICE guidance (NG100) says adults with RA should have access to specialist physiotherapy, with periodic review, to improve general fitness, encourage regular exercise, and learn exercises for joint flexibility and muscle strength. If you have never been offered this, ask your rheumatology nurse or consultant.

A chair helps when your feet, knees or hips make standing painful, when you get tired quickly, or when your balance is not what it was. Seated exercise is still real exercise.

Set up safely before you start

  • Use a firm, stable chair without wheels, ideally with arms, and with your feet flat on the floor.
  • Wear comfortable clothes and supportive shoes or slippers that stay on.
  • Have a drink and your phone within reach.
  • Pick a time of day when you are usually less stiff. For many people with RA that is late morning rather than first thing. If mornings are hard, see easing morning stiffness.
  • If a physiotherapist has given you exercises, follow their plan first. Use this page alongside it, not instead of it.

On a flare day: settle the joints, keep them moving gently

NRAS advises that during a flare, when one or more joints are particularly swollen and tender, it is best to let the joints settle down and do range-of-movement exercises rather than strength training, which puts more strain on the joints. Total bed rest is not the aim either. Gentle movement helps stop stiffness from building up.

  • Move each joint slowly through a comfortable range: shoulder rolls, gentle arm lifts as far as is comfortable, wrist circles, opening and closing your hands, ankle circles and pointing and flexing your feet.
  • Little and often: a few minutes several times a day usually works better than one long session.
  • Stay within comfort: a mild stretch or ache that settles soon afterwards is acceptable. Sharp pain, or a joint that is clearly more swollen afterwards, means you did too much. Do less next time.
  • Leave the hottest joint alone: if one joint is very hot and swollen, rest that joint and keep the others moving.
  • Cold can help: NRAS notes that cold therapy may help reduce joint pain and swelling during a flare. Wrap a cold pack in a cloth, never put it directly on your skin, and take extra care if your skin is thin or your circulation is poor.

Use your flare plan. If you have one from your rheumatology team, follow it. If a flare lasts more than a few days or keeps coming back, contact the team or the advice line. NICE says people with RA should have rapid access to specialist care for flares. For more on getting through a bad week, see surviving a flare week and what to do in a flare.

On better days: build up slowly

Once a flare settles, return to more activity gradually. Start below what you managed before the flare, and add a little at a time. NRAS advises that if an activity seems to make you worse at first, reduce how often you do it and how much, then build up again.

  • Seated strength: knee straightening, pressing your knees together against a cushion, and arm work with a very light weight or a tin, if your hands and wrists allow. The seated strength guide explains how hard this should feel and how to progress.
  • Seated aerobic activity: marching on the spot in your chair, swinging your arms gently or seated tai chi can raise your heart rate a little. See seated tai chi.
  • Getting up and down: practising standing up from your chair keeps everyday strength. See sit-to-stand practice.
  • Next-day check: if your joints are clearly worse the following day, do a bit less next time rather than giving up.

If a long flare or an illness has left you weaker, see rebuilding strength after a flare.

Hands, wrists and feet

RA often affects the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet, so look after them during exercise.

  • Avoid gripping hard. Use padded handles, rest your forearms on the chair arms, or use a looped resistance band instead of holding weights.
  • NICE suggests considering a tailored strengthening and stretching hand exercise programme for adults with RA who have hand or wrist pain and problems with how their hands work. It should be delivered by someone trained in this area. Ask for a referral to a hand therapist or occupational therapist. General ideas are in hand exercises for arthritis.
  • NICE also says adults with RA should have access to an occupational therapist if they have difficulties with everyday activities or hand function, and to a podiatrist if they have foot problems. Insoles and therapeutic footwear should be available if needed.

Fatigue: pace the session

RA fatigue can make exercise feel impossible on some days. Short sessions spread through the day, and stopping before you are exhausted, usually work better than pushing through. Fatigue that is new or getting worse is worth mentioning to your team. See RA fatigue in later life.

Questions to ask your rheumatology team or physiotherapist

  • Can I be referred to a physiotherapist who knows RA?
  • What should I do differently during a flare?
  • Would a hand therapist, occupational therapist or podiatrist help me?
  • Are there any movements I should avoid because of joint damage? NRAS advises supervision from a physiotherapist or experienced exercise professional before starting a new regime if you have a lot of joint damage.

Your regular reviews are a good time to raise these. See RA monitoring in later life.

For family and carers

Encourage little and often rather than one big session. Join in if you can, and help set up a safe chair. Do not push someone to keep going through a hot, swollen joint. Do watch for weeks of not moving at all, because strength can drop quickly.

When to stop and get help

  • Stop and call 999 if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness, or sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body.
  • Get same-day help (GP, rheumatology advice line or NHS 111) if one joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful and you feel feverish or unwell. This can be a joint infection, especially if your medicines lower your immunity.
  • Contact your rheumatology team if flares are frequent, last longer than usual, or exercise keeps making things worse.
  • Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself because of a flare or because you want to exercise more. Ask your team first.

Common questions

Should I rest completely during an RA flare?

Not usually. Rest the hottest, most swollen joints, but keep gently moving the others through a comfortable range, a few minutes at a time. Then build up again as the flare settles.

Can exercise make rheumatoid arthritis worse?

Exercise is recommended for people with RA. Too much, too soon, or strength work on inflamed joints can increase pain for a while. Matching the type of exercise to how your joints are that day is the key, and a physiotherapist can help you plan this.

Is seated exercise enough?

For many people it is a good place to start and a reliable option on bad days. If you can, add some standing practice or walking on better days. If you are not sure, ask your physiotherapist.
